title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A live agent has failed while a client watches. What is the correct order of operations?
options: Patch first so that output resumes quickly, then diagnose and verify afterward
Verify first, then patch the change, then work out what actually caused it
Diagnose first, then patch, then verify the fix against a known-good result
Report to the client first, then patch, then diagnose if there is time
questions.explanation: A fix is a conclusion, not a first action. Patching on top of a wrong diagnosis entangles the failure, so you establish what is true before you change anything and verify after.

questions.question: A delivery stalls suddenly. Where is the failure most likely to live?
options: In a provider or infrastructure link, such as a timeout or an expired key
In the agent's orchestration logic, since that is the code you yourself wrote
In the client's expectations, which have drifted from the delivered scope
In the quality gate, which blocked the run before it could deliver anything
questions.explanation: An agent is a chain of orchestration, provider, tools, and environment, and a sudden stall usually sits in the provider or infrastructure link. Assuming the software is at fault wastes most incident time.

questions.question: Which status message belongs in front of a client during an incident?
options: It should be back up soon, and I will confirm the moment that it is
It is down, I have reproduced the failure, and I will report back in 30 minutes
Everything is fine; the issue is cosmetic and does not affect the output
I do not know what happened yet, so I cannot say anything at all until I do know
questions.explanation: Status reflects actual current state, not a hopeful prediction, and a recurring commitment to report beats one invented timeline. A confident wrong estimate costs more trust than a humble correct one builds.

questions.question: Why is a drive-by change to a live delivery a problem?
options: It is usually much larger than it looks and tends to break the whole build outright
Something now depends on the current behavior, and the change goes unrecorded
It costs considerably more compute to apply than a planned change would
It requires the client's legal team to review and sign a new agreement
questions.explanation: After handover the client's week is built around the current behavior, so a small unrecorded edit alters someone else's operation. A stream of them leaves nobody able to say what the system does.

questions.question: What should be written before a change lands?
options: The rollback plan, specific to the exact prior state
The follow-up change that will improve on it later
The announcement telling the client it already shipped
The estimate of the hours the change consumed
questions.explanation: A change that cannot be reverted cleanly is one you cannot afford to be wrong about. The revert, tied to the precise prior configuration, is written before the change, not improvised after.

questions.question: A change to a job that runs unattended needs what?
options: No gate at all, since no person is present to notice a failure
A gate or check that runs after the change, because no person is watching
A larger scope that bundles in any other tidy-ups while you are already there
A blanket approval mode shared with interactive, human-driven work
questions.explanation: When nothing human is in the loop, the only thing that notices a bad change is an automated guard or eval. What separates a safe change from a dangerous one is often whether anything is watching after it lands.

questions.question: How do the operating doc and the runbook differ?
options: The operating doc is the recovery procedure for failures, and the runbook is the reference for how it is configured
The operating doc is calm reference for configuration, and the runbook is procedure for when it breaks
The operating doc is written for the client, and the runbook is written only for the original builder
The operating doc is written under pressure, and the runbook is written calmly beforehand
questions.explanation: The operating doc answers how the system is put together and configured, read calmly. The runbook answers what to do when something broke, written calmly but read in a hurry by a stranger.

questions.question: How is a handover proven to be real?
options: When the client signs a form confirming that each of the delivered files has been received
When the consultant narrates the demo and the client agrees that the system works
When an unbriefed operator recovers a failed run from the docs while you stay silent
When the documentation has been reviewed and formally approved by the consultant
questions.explanation: Files are not ownership; the ability to run, change, and recover is. The handover passes when a stranger executes the recovery procedure to a successful end without a prompt from you.

questions.question: How should credentials appear in the operating doc?
options: As their actual values, so that the operator can confirm each one directly
As their existence, location, and owner, never their value
Omitted entirely from the doc, so that nothing sensitive is ever written down
As an encrypted block that the operator decrypts whenever it is needed
questions.explanation: The doc records what exists and where it lives so the operator knows what to refresh and whom to ask. Writing the value in turns a configuration note into a breach.

questions.question: An out-of-scope request arrives from one client. What is the right move?
options: Absorb the request quietly so that the client stays happy and never hears about it
Refuse the request bluntly and move on to the work already committed
Offer a re-scope conversation in the client's terms, with the trade and its cost
Delay the request so that the client eventually stops asking about it
questions.explanation: Out-of-scope work is a theft from another client's budget, so it needs a decision. Present it as the client's choice with real costs attached instead of refusing or absorbing silently.

questions.question: Why hold committed utilization below full capacity?
options: To leave room for the guaranteed surprise without abandoning another client
To bill the client for hours that were budgeted but never actually worked at all
To keep the cost of context switching at the maximum possible rate each week
To avoid configuring any client's scheduled work to run unattended
questions.explanation: An urgent issue always arrives, and a portfolio with no slack collapses on the first surprise. Reserved capacity is a deliberate cost of holding several clients, not idle time to sell.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the weekly portfolio review?
options: To measure each client's profit margin against the margins of all the others
To renegotiate every client's contract at the start of each week
To force the whole set into view so a quiet client does not quietly starve
To replace the need for any written scope agreement with any of the clients
questions.explanation: The engagement in front of you always demands attention, and the client you are not looking at is the one that starves. A fixed review forces the whole portfolio into view on a cadence.

questions.question: In the three-layer model of a discipline, which layer carries the transferable value?
options: The implementation layer, the exact syntax of the specific tool being ported
The intent layer, what the discipline is for and what bad outcome it prevents
The configuration layer, the specific set of files that the tool reads at startup
The vendor layer, the platform that the client has standardized on
questions.explanation: The intent survives any tool because it is what the discipline is for. Translation changes the implementation layer and leaves the intent and its mapping untouched.

questions.question: A tool has no primitive that carries an important intent. What should you do?
options: Improvise a fragile approximation and call the translation done
Force the tool to behave like the reference tool until it almost works
Name the capability gap with its price and the client's options
Copy the reference artifact into the tool's format and assume it holds
questions.explanation: An honest capability gap is itself a deliverable with a price and a sign-off. Papering it over leaves an intent that only looks enforced, which is worse than a reported limitation.

questions.question: How do you know a translation actually worked?
options: When every file has been placed correctly in the new tool's expected format
When the intent's bad outcome is still prevented under real use
When the new tool's syntax matches the reference tool's syntax exactly
When the client signs off that the whole migration is complete and closed
questions.explanation: The test is behavior, not artifact: the bad outcome the intent exists to prevent must still be prevented. Files landing in the right place proves nothing about whether the discipline held.
